extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners reviewing §101 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2B) to determine whether claim additional elements amount to an 'inventive concept' (i.e., 'significantly more' than a judicial exception). Focuses on how to identify and evaluate additional elements, consult the specification, and use specific considerations (MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding mere instructions to 'apply it' or implement on a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding the words 'apply it' (or an equivalent) with the judicial exception, or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (e.g., indicating that a particular function such as creating and maintaining electronic records is performed by a computer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such limitations have been found not to be 'significantly more' (see Alice Corp., 134 S. Ct. at 2360; MPEP § 2106.05(f)). Mere statement that a computer performs generic functions does not supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appending well‑understood, routine, conventional activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, to the judicial exception (e.g., a claim to an abstract idea requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-level recitation of conventional computer activity is insufficient to make a claim 'significantly more' (see Alice Corp.; MPEP § 2106.05(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding insignificant extra‑solution activity (mere data gathering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception, e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea (such as obtaining information so it can be analyzed by an abstract mental process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere data gathering or other trivial pre/post‑solution steps do not supply an inventive concept (see CyberSource v. Retail Decisions, Inc.; MPEP § 2106.05(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linking the exception to a technological environment or field of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use (e.g., limiting a mathematical formula to petrochemical fields or saying an abstract idea is used in commodities markets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simply reciting a field of use or technological environment does not make the claim 'significantly more' (see Bilski, Parker; MPEP § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2B; a computer's physical existence alone is not an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Alice: a computer being a tangible system is 'beside the point' — physical implementation alone cannot render a judicial exception patent eligible; conversely, absence of physicality does not automatically doom claims (see Alice, Myriad, Enfish, Genetic Technologies, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B process: identify and evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2B asks whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. Examiners should first identify any additional elements and then evaluate those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the considerations the Supreme Court identified and those in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(h). The evaluation is not a weighing test; examine significance relative to applicant's invention and treat each claim separately. If claim contains multiple discrete exceptions, examiners may select one exception for efficiency, but should avoid parsing a single exception into multiple exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine each claim separately; dependent claims can differ in eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately, based on the particular elements recited; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim may be ineligible while a dependent claim that recites additional elements might be eligible because it amounts to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not parse a single abstract-idea claim into multiple exceptions unless distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple discrete exceptions are clearly present, select one exception and conduct the analysis for that exception; if additional elements amount to significantly more than the selected exception, the claim should be considered eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: improvements to computer functioning or other technology (MPEP §2106.05(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim 'purport(s) to improve the functioning of the computer itself' or 'any other technology or technical field' — i.e., whether the claim searches for a technological solution to a technological problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration may be relevant to Step 2A or Step 2B (or streamlined analyses). Consult precedent (Enfish, McRO, DDR, Amdocs, Visual Memory). To show an improvement, the specification should explain the technical problem and the unconventional technical solution; courts have relied on specification disclosure plus specific claim limitations to find improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must provide a technical explanation of the improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is asserted that the invention improves upon conventional computer functioning or conventional technology, a technical explanation as to how to implement the invention should be present in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure must provide sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing an improvement. Examples: McRO (specification explained how rules enabled automation) vs. Affinity Labs (spec failed to provide implementation details). See MPEP §2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must reflect the improvement under broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining that the specification discloses an improvement, the claim itself must be evaluated to ensure the claim reflects the improvement in technology under its full scope (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claim 'as a whole' and as an 'ordered combination' without ignoring individual step requirements. Avoid oversimplifying claims. Examples: Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec (claims didn't reflect alleged improvement even if specification argued so); McRO discussion of evaluating claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement must be a particular solution (not merely an idea or outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: An important consideration is the extent to which the claim covers a particular solution to a problem or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome, as opposed to merely claiming the idea of a solution or outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration overlaps with 'particular machine' and 'mere instructions to apply' considerations (see DDR, McRO). Claims that specify particular ways or structures to achieve results are more likely to be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method claims must be limited to computer implementation to show computer improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a method claim to improve computer functionality, the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim must be limited to computer implementation; if the entire scope can be performed mentally or verbally, it cannot be said to improve computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Synopsys (entire steps could be performed mentally — ineligible), RecogniCorp (process could be practiced verbally or without a computer — ineligible). Ensure claim scope requires computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that may show an improvement in computer functionality or technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative examples courts have indicated may show improvements: modification of hyperlink protocol to produce hybrid webpage (DDR); inventive distribution of network functionality for filtering (BASCOM); methods of rendering halftone images; distributed network architectures reducing congestion; configurable memory systems; technical details for transmitting images over cellular networks; particular server structures for organized digital images; specific software programming/design creating menus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are precedential illustrations where courts found improvements — examiners should compare claim and specification facts to these types of features when evaluating Step 2A/2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples that courts have indicated may not be sufficient to show improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative examples courts found insufficient: generating restaurant menus with functional features (Ameranth); accelerating analysis only by virtue of general-purpose computer speed (FairWarning); merely using a computer to perform an abstract idea (Return Mail); mere automation of manual processes (Credit Acceptance, LendingTree); recording/transmitting/archiving digital images using conventional technology without inventive solution (TLI Communications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are counter-examples: claiming conventional computer use, automation, or relying solely on general-purpose computer capacity typically fails to provide 'significantly more.' Examiners should be wary of such fact patterns.
